Give the I–V curves of the two subcells — top and bottom — and get the full two-terminal tandem result in seconds. Built for perovskite/silicon and other tandem solar cell work, including SCAPS-1D output.

Two-terminal series — same current through both subcells, voltages add.
Split spectrum: this combine assumes both curves belong to the same tandem under the split spectrum — the top cell under full sunlight, and the bottom cell measured under the light filtered by the top cell. If both curves were measured or simulated separately under the full spectrum, the bottom-cell current will be too high and the efficiency will be overestimated.

Optical filter calculator (estimate)

No filtered bottom-cell curve? Estimate the correction factor from the top cell instead. The estimate treats the top cell as a step absorber at its bandgap, with Beer–Lambert leakage exp(−α·d) for light above the bandgap, using standard AM1.5G photon currents. It is an estimate only — a real filtered simulation (for example in SCAPS-1D) is more accurate.

4-terminal result (mechanically stacked)

In a 4-terminal tandem each subcell works on its own, at its own maximum power point — the powers simply add, and no current matching is needed. Same data as the 2-terminal result above, so you can compare the two directly.

Parasitic resistances — Rs and Rsh

Estimated from the slope of each curve: series resistance Rs = −dV/dJ near Voc, shunt resistance Rsh = −dV/dJ near Jsc. Estimates for your results section — check them against your simulator's own values when you have them.

DeviceRs (Ω·cm²)Rsh (Ω·cm²)

Computed vs measured tandem

Difference = (computed − measured) ÷ measured × 100. Small differences mean the subcell curves and the real tandem agree.

Publication table export

The comparison table above, ready for a paper: LaTeX (booktabs) to paste into a manuscript, a tab-separated copy that pastes straight into Word or Excel as a table, or a Word file download.

Shockley–Queisser (SQ) limit comparison

Enter the subcell bandgaps. The single-junction SQ limits are interpolated from standard detailed-balance values (AM1.5G, 300 K, approximate). The tandem SQ figure is an estimate for a current-matched pair (top cell thinned to match currents, radiative-limit voltages, fill factor 0.89) — a guide, not an exact detailed-balance run.

Temperature estimateEstimate only

ESTIMATE ONLY — not a replacement for a SCAPS-1D run at that temperature. The 25 °C tandem result is scaled with typical perovskite/silicon tandem temperature coefficients (edit them if you have measured ones). Real behaviour — phase changes, contact effects, hysteresis — is not included.

Batch, EQE & saved projects

Work with many runs at once, integrate an EQE curve, and keep your results.

Batch processing — many I–V files at once

Upload up to 20 files in total — for example the top-cell runs of a SCAPS-1D batch (thickness sweep) plus the bottom-cell file. Files are paired in filename order; a single file on one side is reused for every file on the other side. Each pair is combined with exactly the same calculation as the main tool.

EQE — integrated Jsc from an EQE curve

Paste or upload an EQE curve — two columns: wavelength (nm), EQE (% or 0–1). The integrated Jsc uses an embedded approximate AM1.5G photon spectrum built into this page, so treat it as a close estimate: for a paper, integrate against your measured or simulator spectrum. Filtered (bottom-cell) EQE gives the filtered Jsc the same way.

How the combination works

1 · Series rule

In a two-terminal tandem the same current flows through both subcells. At any current, the tandem voltage is the top-cell voltage plus the bottom-cell voltage at that same current.

2 · Common current grid

Both curves are interpolated onto one shared current grid, from zero up to the smaller of the two short-circuit currents. That smaller current becomes the tandem Jsc — the weaker subcell limits the device.

3 · Result

Adding the voltages point by point gives the tandem I–V curve. Voc is the sum of the two subcell Voc values, and the maximum of V × J gives Pmax, the fill factor and the efficiency.
